claims.claim: The microbit.org 'Introduction to the micro:bit' unit structures every lesson on a recurring Think -> Create -> Evaluate -> Extend -> Share arc, a pattern reproduced verbatim in the L1-s2..s6 decks per their R0 provenance delta fields.

For a young-kids track the Think phase should open each session with one concrete physical micro:bit artefact (e.g., a name badge or beating heart on the LED matrix) so abstract code is anchored to a tangible object, which Merrill's First Principles identify as the basis for effective demonstration and application.
Reduce extraneous cognitive load on young learners by presenting one idea per slide and chunking the Create phase into small build steps, per Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory.

Age-appropriate pacing for a young-kids track should shorten reflective Evaluate/Extend segments and interleave frequent hands-on physical interaction with the device rather than long teacher-talk, consistent with Universal Design for Learning's call for multiple, flexible means of engagement.

The Share phase for young kids should have them physically show their micro:bit artefact to peers rather than complete written reflection, satisfying the relatedness and competence needs that Self-Determination Theory ties to motivation.

All six L1 sessions currently omit the upstream's differentiated support/challenge and assessment guidance (R0 missing[]/dropped[]), so the kids-track adaptation must re-insert age-appropriate differentiation and success criteria into the Evaluate/Extend phases of the model.
